## Model specification and estimation {#sec-ch4-supp-spec}

The primary model (M4) was selected from nested models that differed in how physical effort, stimulus type and task entered drift and boundary separation (@tbl-ch4-formulas). M0 had no physical effort terms on drift or boundary separation. M1 added physical effort to both, and M2 let those effects vary with task difficulty. M3 instead added the physical effort × stimulus term to drift in M1, and M4 also let drift and boundary separation differ between tasks. Allowing drift and boundary separation to differ between tasks improved out-of-sample prediction (M4 vs. M3: `r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M3_vs_M4", "se_delta_elpd_M3_vs_M4", flip = TRUE)`), whereas allowing the physical effort effects to differ between tasks did not (M4b vs. M4: `r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M4b_vs_M4", "se_delta_elpd_M4b_vs_M4")`; @tbl-ch4-model-comparison). Two variants of M4 tested the robustness of its physical effort effects: M4b added physical effort × task interactions on drift, and M4r added by-participant random slopes for physical effort on drift and boundary separation.

The starting point did not depend on stimulus type, which could not be known before the trial. Boundary separation was allowed to vary with stimulus type to absorb RT differences between stimulus types; because stimulus types were intermixed, these terms are not interpreted as strategic settings (@sec-ch4-4-5). Non-decision time had no predictors because, in a delayed-response design, it mainly absorbs the delay before the cue.

The boundary-separation intercept was bounded between 0.3 and 5, and non-decision time between 0.02 s and 0.01 s below the shortest RT. Sampling used adapt_delta = `r fmt_num(v("adapt_delta"), 2)` and a maximum tree depth of `r v("max_treedepth")`. `r v("refit_models")` did not meet the convergence criterion at `r fmt_int(v("n_iter"))` iterations and were refit with `r fmt_int(v("n_iter_refit"))` iterations. In the leave-one-out comparisons, observations with Pareto *k* > 0.7 were handled with moment matching and exact refits.

For the full pupil sample, the comparison model was P0, the primary model fit to that sample, which also gave the physical effort effects in that sample (@tbl-ch4-pupil-models). Pupil measures with their own valid-data requirement (the pre-squeeze baseline, the previous trial's TEPR, the pre-response window and the grip period), and the sample without the slowest trials, each had a baseline model fit to the same trials (@tbl-ch4-formulas).

@tbl-ch4-priors lists the priors, @tbl-ch4-formulas the formula of every model and @tbl-ch4-convergence the convergence diagnostics.

## Model comparison and primary-model estimates

@tbl-ch4-model-comparison compares the nested models by PSIS-LOO, and @tbl-ch4-m2-interactions gives the task difficulty × physical effort terms of M2. @tbl-ch4-fixef-m4 and @tbl-ch4-condition-cells give the primary model's population-level estimates and its condition-level drift and boundary separation. Relative to Identical trials, boundary separation was narrower on Hard (`r eff("diff_hard_bs", pct = TRUE)`) and Easy trials (`r eff("diff_easy_bs", pct = TRUE)`), and it did not differ between tasks (`r eff("task_bs", rope = TRUE)`).

## Model adequacy

The primary model reproduced choice proportions closely (@tbl-ch4-ppc-choice; @fig-ch4-ppc, panel A). RT quantiles fit less well: observed RTs for minority responses were slower than predicted (@fig-ch4-ppc, panel B), the pattern expected when across-trial variability in drift is not modeled. The non-decision-time posterior lay well below its upper bound (@fig-ch4-ndt).

::: {#fig-ch4-ppc}

```{r}

#| out-width: "100%"
suppressWarnings(knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(params$figures_dir, "S_ppc_M4.png"), mustWork = TRUE), error = FALSE))
```


Pupil measures by task and physical effort. The TEPR is shown relative to the pre-probe and to the pre-squeeze baseline; grip-period pupil size is relative to the pre-squeeze baseline

:::

Each participant × task cell contained trials at both physical effort levels (median `r av("cell_median")` per level, minimum `r av("cell_min")`; `r av("cells_lt10")` of `r av("cells_total")` cells had fewer than 10 trials at one level). Pupil predictors were centered within participant × task × physical effort, so each cell mean rested on at least `r av("cell_min")` trials. Counts per physical effort level and stimulus type were smaller (median `r av("cell_stim_median")`, minimum `r av("cell_stim_min")`), but the pupil predictors were not centered within stimulus type, so these smaller counts do not affect the centering. @tbl-ch4-pupil-sensitivity repeats the physical effort comparisons of pupil size with at least 10 or 15 trials per physical effort level, with trial counts equalized between levels by random subsampling (1,000 draws), and with a trial-level mixed model. With at least 15 trials per level, the VDT difference in the TEPR relative to the pre-probe baseline was no longer significant (*p* = `r av("vdt_tepr_k15_p")`). @fig-ch4-grip-participants shows each participant's grip-period pupil size at both physical effort levels.

::: {#tbl-ch4-pupil-sensitivity}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ch3_tbl_pupil_sensitivity()
```

Sensitivity of the physical effort comparisons of pupil size to the number of trials per participant. *M*diff is high minus low physical effort in arbitrary units. Equalized counts: within each participant and task, the physical effort level with more trials was randomly subsampled to the count of the other, 1,000 times. Trial-level model: linear mixed model with a by-participant intercept, and a slope for physical effort where it was estimable. For the ADT grip period, the trial-level model has a random intercept only, because the model with a random slope was singular.

:::

::: {#fig-ch4-grip-participants}


Grip-period pupil size (1.00–4.35 s after squeeze onset) for each participant at low and high physical effort. Lines join each participant's two means; large points are group means with 95% confidence intervals.

## Behavioral mixed-effects models

These models analyze observed accuracy and median RT directly. The accuracy contrasts reported in @sec-ch4-3-1 come from the first of them.

Random slopes for physical effort were singular on both the accuracy and the median-RT models, so each model uses a random intercept only, `r v("acc_model_re")`, following @Barr2013-maximal, @bates2015parsimonious, and @Brauer2018-lmm.

::: {#tbl-ch4-reduction}

## Analysis provenance

Pupil samples were placed on a time axis at the recorded 250-Hz sampling rate, from 3 s before squeeze onset to the end of the confidence window. Earlier internal analyses that used a time axis derived from file timestamps were discarded, because that axis compressed time and misplaced the analysis windows; no result from those analyses is reported.
